title: “From Prompt to Film” — An AI-Empowered Micro-Film Studio
introHtml:
Project: “From Prompt to Film” — An AI-Empowered Micro-Film Studio

UNNC GRP Team202610 combines visual-model research, data preparation, application development, and video-editing experience relevant to P30. Ziqian XIONG's computer-vision research, 3D/4D reconstruction work, and interactive software projects provide a starting point for visual-model experiments and integration. Yun Xin NG brings dataset preparation and model evaluation, while Jinyao LU's LLM-related research, scriptwriting, and video editing connect with story development and final composition. The team's programming, annotation, and CI/CD skills support the wider workflow.

We want to build a studio that turns a story premise into a watchable film with consistent characters, voiceover, music, and subtitles. Our initial demonstration will use one character and four to eight shots in a 30–60-second film, allowing us to test the complete process before increasing duration and complexity.

Ziqian XIONG will coordinate model comparisons, shared learning, and early supervisor feedback. We will check GPU capacity and model licences early, develop bounded training/adaptation experiments, and connect the results through a web application with preview and shot-level retry. Technical checks and viewer feedback will guide improvements to visual coherence, narrative alignment, and reliable playback.

teamIntroHtml:
Our seven-member team, led by Ziqian XIONG, combines data preparation and model evaluation, algorithm implementation, application and database development, and testing, deployment, and user communication. We will connect these strengths through shared data definitions, module interfaces, and integration reviews so that experimental results become demonstrable software. The following profiles present the experience supporting our project plan; responsibilities are set out in the work-distribution section.

We believe that the bidding groups have broadly comparable academic foundations. We therefore see stronger leadership and proactive engagement as our competitive advantage: a leader who can guide shared learning and coordinate decisions, and members willing to investigate unfamiliar methods, raise difficulties early, and follow through on feedback. We will put this into practice through weekly progress reviews during concentrated development, paired method discussions, and early demonstrations; the low-workload period will use brief asynchronous check-ins.

proposalHtml:
Project Proposal

We will develop a web studio that turns a story premise, genre, language, and visual style into a downloadable MP4 with voiceover, background music, and embedded subtitles. Users will review structured storyboards and character references, follow generation progress, preview clips, and regenerate individual shots. The workflow will connect script generation, video synthesis, character consistency, audio generation, and automated editing.

The first integrated milestone will be a single-character, four-to-eight-shot film lasting 30–60 seconds. The delivery target is a coherent one-to-two-minute film; longer films and additional characters will build on measured GPU capacity and output quality. Training and adaptation will form part of the implementation, with lightweight fine-tuning or LoRA and reproducible records of datasets, base models, configurations, and weight versions. Deliverables will include the preprocessing pipeline, model weights and architecture descriptions for the script, video, character-consistency, and audio modules, evaluation reports, the integrated application, installation and usage documentation, and a maintenance plan. External service integration will be documented separately from trained components.
technicalHtml:
1. Back-end Development

    Python and FastAPI will expose project, storyboard, generation, preview, retry, and export APIs. Celery and Redis will queue GPU and composition tasks; SQLite will store project metadata and task states, while file storage will hold versioned media assets. Each task will record its inputs, model version, seed where supported, timing, output assets, and failure reason.

    PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers/Diffusers will support script and video models, lightweight adaptation, and reference-image conditioning. A validated JSON schema will define scenes, characters, actions, dialogue, camera descriptions, and durations. Character profiles will combine authorised reference images and consistent descriptions. Reference conditioning and adaptation will be compared against unadapted baselines using fixed evaluation stories. OpenCV will check frames and visual outputs.

    Mandarin/English speech synthesis and music-generation modules will supply dialogue and emotional background tracks. FFmpeg will assemble approved clips, transitions, mixed audio, and subtitles, and ffprobe will verify the final container, tracks, and duration. Failed shots will be retried independently; replacing a shot will invalidate only the dependent composition tasks.

  2. Front-end Development

    React and TypeScript will provide story entry, genre/style and language controls, storyboard and character review, task progress, clip previews, local regeneration, and MP4 download. API responses will identify processing stages and failed shots so that users can resume work without restarting the entire film.

Evaluation and delivery: The opening resource trial will measure GPU memory, runtime, storage, and model access before adaptation experiments. Evaluation will combine CLIP score for prompt alignment, FID for distribution-level visual comparison on suitable evaluation sets, character-consistency checks, narrative review, user preference ratings, inference latency, and failure-case analysis. Neither visual metric alone will establish film quality. Licensed training data, model and asset records, visible AI-generated-content marks, containerised deployment, model cards, and documented update and recovery procedures will support delivery.

Core data flow: Story and style → screenplay/storyboard JSON → character references and video shots → voiceover/music/subtitles → FFmpeg composition → playback and quality checks → marked MP4 export.
timelineIntroHtml:
Ziqian XIONG will lead weekly progress and integration reviews during concentrated development and use brief asynchronous check-ins in the low-workload period. Paired discussions of methods and code, and early demonstrations, will support supervisor feedback. The leader will help members break down unfamiliar tasks and resolve dependencies. Each member will prepare questions, report blockers early, and record decisions and follow-up actions.

The project runs from 21 October 2026 to final submission on 1 April 2027, with work organised by date ranges, workload, and demonstrable outputs. We use 16 December 2026–5 January 2027 to review documents and finish earlier tasks as needed. As January and February may overlap the winter vacation, 6 January–28 February is a low-workload period: at most one small asynchronous task per member per week, adjusted to availability, with no critical integration, required training runs, or participant trials. University holiday dates remain subject to formal notices. We bring the first demonstrable workflow and pilot experiments forward to 15 December, complete integration and evaluation in March, and reserve 31 March–1 April for submission checks.

Course milestones follow the supplied tentative key-dates table, subject to formal course notices.

phases.name: Requirements, GPU & licences
tasks: Agree the story-to-film workflow, single-character first scope, and output standards. Check model and data licences, trial script, video, character-reference, and audio candidates, and measure GPU memory, runtime, and storage needs.

Prepare GPU/storage requests from 21 October. Submit ethics forms by 28 October, covering licensed training assets, faces/voices, synthetic-content disclosure, consent, and planned viewer trials; begin participant work only after the required approval.

phases.name: Storyboard, queue & baseline
tasks: Publish the team project website by 5 November, with the scope and licensed or synthetic examples. Design storyboard JSON, character records, asset versions, FastAPI contracts, and Celery/Redis task states.

Prepare licensed assets and preprocessing scripts, check screenplay and storyboard output, and connect the video baseline to the task queue. By 24 November, generate a playable clip from a story, show failed tasks, and support shot-level retry. Prepare interface skeletons and reusable evaluation samples in parallel.

phases.name: First film & adaptation pilots
tasks: Add character references, initial Mandarin/English voice, music, subtitles, and FFmpeg editing. By 15 December, demonstrate a playable single-character, four-to-eight-shot, 30–60-second film, including shot replacement and recomposition through a development interface. Mark the film as AI-generated and retain model and asset versions.

In parallel, run a bounded licensed fine-tuning/LoRA pilot within measured GPU capacity and prepare web-studio skeletons, fixed test prompts, and evaluation scripts. Submit the interim report by 10 December, using evidence available then; archive configurations, permitted weights, outputs, and failures by 15 December.

phases.name: Review & documentation
tasks: Use this time to review documents, collect feedback, and finish earlier tasks as needed; no critical work or participant trials are scheduled. Low-workload activity continues from 6 January.

phases.name: Low-workload review
tasks: Review saved pilot clips, subtitle timing, licence/asset records, and failure examples in small independent tasks. Draft model cards, prompt guidance, and installation notes using existing outputs; require no new training or GPU-dependent deliverable.

Use asynchronous check-ins to maintain the issue list and prepare viewer-review forms and March priorities. Make no web-studio delivery commitment in January or February; resume concentrated integration on 1 March.

phases.name: Studio integration
tasks: Complete the existing story-input, progress, storyboard-review, preview, and download pages. Connect shot regeneration to the task service; check bilingual audio/subtitle timing, cancellation, retries, and updates to affected assets after replacing a shot.

By 9 March, demonstrate story entry, generation, preview, shot replacement, and MP4 export. Select models using the December pilot results, retain baseline and adaptation records, and explain which modules use trained models or external services. Add no new long training runs.

phases.name: Quality, cost & viewer trials
tasks: Use the prepared prompts, including unseen genres, to compare baseline and adapted outputs for narrative fit and character consistency. Report CLIP alignment and FID on suitable evaluation sets; run approved viewer trials and record preferences and audio/visual failures.

Measure latency, success rate, GPU use, per-film cost, queue load, cancellation, and recovery in parallel. By 16 March, assess the coherent one-to-two-minute target against measured quality/resources and document any scope adjustment agreed with the supervisor.

phases.name: Release, report & demonstration
tasks: Freeze features/models on 17 March, regress representative prompts, bilingual subtitles, local regeneration, and playback, and validate GPU deployment in a fresh environment by 23 March. Complete model cards, permitted weight access, APIs, and maintenance/recovery instructions.

Use 24–30 March to rehearse the story-to-MP4 demonstration with actual generation timing and clearly labelled backup films. Complete the application, final report, permitted model package, evaluation records, and documentation by 30 March.

phases.name: Submission checks
tasks: Verify release/report/documentation consistency, filenames, access, and receipts; submit the team final report and software by 1 April. Prepare demonstration, presentation, and promotional assets for later course submissions.

workHtml:
We will divide the work according to our relevant experience and interests, help one another learn unfamiliar methods, and adjust tasks through progress discussions and supervisor feedback.

  • Ziqian XIONG: Coordinate the team, supervisor discussions, and GPU planning; guide system design, video-model experiments, and character-consistency checks, drawing on his visual-computing and integration experience.
  • Yun Xin NG: Prepare text, video, and reference-image datasets, compare candidate models, and support training and evaluation, drawing on her data-preparation and model-evaluation experience.
  • Jinyao LU: Review storyboards, develop the audio, subtitle, and final-composition workflow, and organise demonstration stories and viewer feedback, drawing on his scriptwriting and video-editing experience.
  • Oswald Yiwen CHONG: Develop backend tasks and asset storage, connect generation stages, and support failure recovery, automated checks, and deployment.
  • Ziqian ZHANG: Organise character references and shot annotations, check asset consistency, and record visual artifacts and failed cases, building on her annotation and data-preparation experience.
  • Yue WU: Develop and check structured screenplay and storyboard formats, compare script-generation methods, and document prompt and adaptation experiments with the team.
  • Xinyun HU: Build story-input, style-selection, progress, preview, and download pages; connect them to task services and check shot regeneration and retry interactions.

Ziqian XIONG and Yun Xin NG will work together on model experiments; Yue WU and Jinyao LU will check the connection between scripts, shots, and sound. Members will learn unfamiliar generation and editing tools through small joint experiments.

fit.title: Visual-computing research to support generative experiments
fit.body: Ziqian XIONG's medical image segmentation research and 4DGS-Edit-and-Compare project provide relevant preparation in image processing, model comparison, and inspection of visual outputs. Jinyao LU's LLM-related research provides a foundation for discussing script-generation methods. We will learn and validate video generation, character consistency, and narrative alignment through literature review and controlled experiments.

fit.title: A complete workflow around the models
fit.body: Yun Xin NG's model training and dataset preparation and Ziqian ZHANG's image/JSON annotation experience can support training and evaluation materials. Yue WU's programming and research-analysis background can support structured scripts and method comparison. Xinyun HU's application foundations and Oswald Yiwen CHONG's application and CI/CD experience support the user interface, task integration, automated checks, and deployment.

fit.title: Early validation of generative-model feasibility
fit.body: We will build on our visual-model and benchmarking experience through an early GPU/model trial and targeted learning of the selected PyTorch, Transformers, and video-processing tools. The first milestone will demonstrate a controlled short-film workflow; training/adaptation evidence, quality, runtime, and resource findings will guide subsequent implementation and quality improvements.

conclusionHtml:
Our team brings research related to computer vision and LLMs together with dataset preparation, application development, and delivery automation. We will extend this preparation through targeted learning and experiments to address the need for both a coherent story and a reliable prompt-to-film workflow. We will test model and GPU feasibility early, demonstrate a controlled short film, and use technical checks and viewer feedback to guide iteration. Through staged implementation and supervisor reviews, we will deliver an application whose creative outputs can be generated, inspected, reproduced where supported, and demonstrated end to end.

Building on our academic preparation, we aim to distinguish our team through stronger leadership and peer guidance, proactive learning, and consistent follow-through throughout the project.

Ideas & Design

Project Proposal

We will develop a web studio that turns a story premise, genre, language, and visual style into a downloadable MP4 with voiceover, background music, and embedded subtitles. Users will review structured storyboards and character references, follow generation progress, preview clips, and regenerate individual shots. The workflow will connect script generation, video synthesis, character consistency, audio generation, and automated editing.

The first integrated milestone will be a single-character, four-to-eight-shot film lasting 30–60 seconds. The delivery target is a coherent one-to-two-minute film; longer films and additional characters will build on measured GPU capacity and output quality. Training and adaptation will form part of the implementation, with lightweight fine-tuning or LoRA and reproducible records of datasets, base models, configurations, and weight versions. Deliverables will include the preprocessing pipeline, model weights and architecture descriptions for the script, video, character-consistency, and audio modules, evaluation reports, the integrated application, installation and usage documentation, and a maintenance plan. External service integration will be documented separately from trained components.

Technology Stack & System Design

  1. Back-end Development

    Python and FastAPI will expose project, storyboard, generation, preview, retry, and export APIs. Celery and Redis will queue GPU and composition tasks; SQLite will store project metadata and task states, while file storage will hold versioned media assets. Each task will record its inputs, model version, seed where supported, timing, output assets, and failure reason.

    PyTorch and Hugging Face Transformers/Diffusers will support script and video models, lightweight adaptation, and reference-image conditioning. A validated JSON schema will define scenes, characters, actions, dialogue, camera descriptions, and durations. Character profiles will combine authorised reference images and consistent descriptions. Reference conditioning and adaptation will be compared against unadapted baselines using fixed evaluation stories. OpenCV will check frames and visual outputs.

    Mandarin/English speech synthesis and music-generation modules will supply dialogue and emotional background tracks. FFmpeg will assemble approved clips, transitions, mixed audio, and subtitles, and ffprobe will verify the final container, tracks, and duration. Failed shots will be retried independently; replacing a shot will invalidate only the dependent composition tasks.

  2. Front-end Development

    React and TypeScript will provide story entry, genre/style and language controls, storyboard and character review, task progress, clip previews, local regeneration, and MP4 download. API responses will identify processing stages and failed shots so that users can resume work without restarting the entire film.

Evaluation and delivery: The opening resource trial will measure GPU memory, runtime, storage, and model access before adaptation experiments. Evaluation will combine CLIP score for prompt alignment, FID for distribution-level visual comparison on suitable evaluation sets, character-consistency checks, narrative review, user preference ratings, inference latency, and failure-case analysis. Neither visual metric alone will establish film quality. Licensed training data, model and asset records, visible AI-generated-content marks, containerised deployment, model cards, and documented update and recovery procedures will support delivery.

Core data flow: Story and style → screenplay/storyboard JSON → character references and video shots → voiceover/music/subtitles → FFmpeg composition → playback and quality checks → marked MP4 export.

Conclusion

Our team brings research related to computer vision and LLMs together with dataset preparation, application development, and delivery automation. We will extend this preparation through targeted learning and experiments to address the need for both a coherent story and a reliable prompt-to-film workflow. We will test model and GPU feasibility early, demonstrate a controlled short film, and use technical checks and viewer feedback to guide iteration. Through staged implementation and supervisor reviews, we will deliver an application whose creative outputs can be generated, inspected, reproduced where supported, and demonstrated end to end.

Building on our academic preparation, we aim to distinguish our team through stronger leadership and peer guidance, proactive learning, and consistent follow-through throughout the project.
